title: Isolated facial diplegia: A rare presentation of Guillain‐Barre syndrome
case_prompt:
A 34‐year‐old man with no past medical history presented with a 1‐day history of sudden‐onset numbness and heaviness of the tongue, drooling of saliva, loss of taste, slurring of speech, and the inability to close both eyes completely. He denied earache, hearing changes, tinnitus, head or neck trauma, fever, flu‐like symptoms, gastrointestinal complaints, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, altered consciousness, or limb weakness or numbness. He had no recent travel, sick contacts, insect bites, or use of herbal supplements; he did not smoke or use alcohol or illicit drugs.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Neurologically, visual fields and acuity were intact; pupils were equal and reactive; extraocular movements were full without diplopia. Bilateral lagophthalmos with Bell’s phenomenon was noted. He was unable to clench his teeth, blow, whistle, frown his forehead, or show his teeth; nasolabial folds were absent bilaterally. Facial sensation and jaw strength were normal. Hearing, palate movement, head rotation, and shoulder shrug were intact. Deep tendon reflexes were diminished (1/4) in all limbs with absent ankle jerks. Motor strength, tone, bulk, and sensation in the extremities were normal. The remainder of the systemic examination was unremarkable.

Routine blood counts and metabolic panel were unremarkable. Serum ANA, anti-dsDNA, and ANCA were within normal limits. PCR assays for herpes and CMV, EBV viral capsid antigen, Quantiferon TB, and serologies for HIV and Lyme disease were all negative. CSF analysis showed albuminocytological dissociation without pleocytosis or organisms. Non-contrast CT of the head was normal. MRI brain with contrast and intracranial MRA revealed no abnormalities. Chest radiograph, CT chest, and PET–CT scan were negative for lymphoma, malignancy, sarcoidosis, or paraneoplastic processes. EMG and nerve conduction studies demonstrated a demyelinating pattern of facial neuropathy, and the blink reflex study was abnormal bilaterally.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bell’s palsy was considered but bilateral involvement and systemic signs argued against it — “Most cases of unilateral LMN facial nerve palsy are idiopathic, referred to as Bell’s palsy. However, cases of bilateral LMN facial nerve palsy are predominantly attributed to underlying systemic conditions.”  
2. Viral etiologies (herpes, CMV, EBV) were excluded by negative PCR assays — “PCR examination of the blood for herpes and cytomegalovirus (CMV) viruses, viral capsid antigen for EBV… were all negative.”  
3. Lyme disease was excluded by negative serology — “…serological tests of HIV, and Lyme disease were all negative.”  
4. Sarcoidosis and malignancy were excluded by whole-body PET–CT and CT chest — “CT chest and whole-body positron emission tomography (PET) CT scan did not reveal any evidence of underlying lymphoma, malignancy, sarcoidosis, or other paraneoplastic causes.”  
5. Intracranial lesions and encephalitis were excluded by normal head CT, MRI brain with contrast, and intracranial MRA — “A non-contrast CT scan of the head showed no intra- or extracranial pathology. MRI brain with contrast and intracranial MRA were normal…”  
6. Tuberculous meningitis was excluded by negative Quantiferon TB and negative CSF AFB smear and culture — “Quantiferon TB… CSF AFB Smear, PCR, and Culture Negative.”  
7. HIV-associated and cryptococcal meningitis were excluded by negative HIV serology and sterile CSF culture — “serological tests of HIV… CSF Culture Negative.”  
8. Guillain–Barré syndrome variant was supported by albuminocytologic dissociation, demyelinating nerve conduction findings, and abnormal blink reflex — “Analysis of cerebrospinal fluid showed albuminocytological dissociation with no evidence of infection” and “EMG and nerve conduction velocity (NCV) revealed a demyelinating type of facial palsy.”
